rows.text:
About TradeHQ

TradeHQ exists to make financial education more accessible through practical learning. It is an educational simulator — not a brokerage, not an advisor.

Mission

Make financial literacy practical. TradeHQ lets anyone learn how markets work by doing — users manually place simulated market buys and sells, watch portfolios respond to news and price action, and study the outcomes without risking a single dollar.

Vision

A world where the first exposure to trading is educational, not expensive. Beginners should be able to make — and learn from — their first thousand mistakes on a simulator, not on their savings.

Educational Philosophy

Worked examples and virtual exercises complement reading. Every feature — the $100,000 virtual portfolio, the educational mentor, the daily challenge, the wiki and the compound growth simulator — exists to turn abstract concepts (risk, position sizing, diversification, psychology) into things you can feel through hands-on practice.

Open the hypothetical compound growth calculator

Transparency

TradeHQ is not a brokerage. We do not custody funds, execute real trades, or provide financial advice. Prices shown are simulated or delayed and are for education only. Third-party advertising and optional analytics are described in the privacy policy; their operation depends on provider settings and applicable user choices.

Technology

TradeHQ is a modern web application built with React, TypeScript and a serverless backend. Guest practice records stay in your browser so you can start without signing up. Account cash, positions and server-recorded trades restore across devices when available; earlier guest trade history and journals remain browser-held; signed-in lessons and beginner-journey progress can sync privately when online. The standalone mentor uses a built-in answer library and local topic matching without an AI API request; portfolio mentor tools can use simulated portfolio context.

Creator

TradeHQ was created by Anuga Weerasinghe as an educational software project focused on helping beginners understand financial markets through simulation and structured learning.

What TradeHQ Is Not
Not a brokerage — no real orders are ever routed to any exchange.
Not a financial or investment advisor — nothing on the site is a recommendation to buy or sell.
Not a source of live, guaranteed market data — prices are simulated or delayed for education.
Not a substitute for professional advice — talk to a licensed advisor before investing real money.
How the material is written and reviewed

TradeHQ uses AI-assisted drafting and editing for educational material and software. Checks include worked-example arithmetic, consistency with simulator features and source suitability within the scope recorded on each page. These checks do not establish that every statement is correct or independently reviewed by a professional. References may provide background rather than evidence that a strategy predicts prices. Options and futures lessons are conceptual; the simulator does not execute those contracts.

Community Reviews publish visitor-submitted feedback; we do not independently verify reviewers' identities or experiences. The Community Practice Board publishes optional, server-recorded ranked simulated portfolios, with earlier browser-reported results labelled separately. These are not independently verified investment results. Neither feedback nor practice rankings promise real-world returns. Educational figures use cited sources or clearly labelled hypothetical examples; when a question has no honest answer — which asset will rise, whether a strategy will work for you — the page says so instead of guessing. Content is revised whenever a reader points out an error or a market mechanism changes, and corrections are made in place rather than quietly removed.

TradeHQ is an educational paper trading simulator. No real money is traded. Nothing on this website constitutes investment, financial, legal or tax advice. Past simulated performance does not predict future real-world performance.

What is Head and Shoulders?

Published by TradeHQ. Site creator and editorial approach: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date.

A head and shoulders pattern has three peaks, with a higher central peak and two lower shoulders. A neckline connects the intervening lows; breaking it is a chart observation, not a confirmed future decline or guaranteed target.

DETAILED DEFINITION

The head and shoulders pattern is a commonly described reversal formation in technical analysis. It consists of three distinct peaks: a left shoulder, a higher central peak (the head), and a right shoulder that is approximately equal in height to the left shoulder. The troughs between these peaks are connected by a line called the neckline, and a break below this neckline completes the conventional pattern description; continued decline is a hypothesis that can fail. The conventional description follows five price phases; these observations do not establish participant motives. Phase one: the market trends upward and creates the left shoulder, a normal swing high. Phase two: a pullback creates the first neckline touch. Phase three: renewed buying pushes price to a higher high (the head), suggesting the uptrend is accelerating. Phase four: another pullback returns to the neckline area, and bulls attempt one more push higher. Phase five: the rally fails to reach the head's height, forming the right shoulder — a lower peak that some analysts interpret as weakening upward momentum. The measured move technique provides a price target: measure the vertical distance from the head to the neckline, then subtract that distance from the neckline breakout point. Volume adds a separate historical observation; it does not validate a forecast. Some descriptions compare volume across the shoulders, head and neckline break. State the observation window and volume source; a lower volume does not by itself establish participants’ conviction or predict the next move. Volume alone does not establish the probability that a neckline break will persist. The inverse pattern uses three troughs rather than peaks and is commonly interpreted as a bullish hypothesis, which can fail.

KEY POINTS
Three peaks: left shoulder, head (highest), right shoulder
A neckline break describes the chart; a measured target is a projection, not a guaranteed outcome
The inverse shape can occur without a lasting upward reversal
💡 WHY THIS MATTERS

Draw the three peaks and neckline, then distinguish the pattern's measured-move convention from the actual later price. A projected target is a hypothesis rather than an expected payout.

Worked exercise and its limits

Mark three hypothetical peaks at $50, $55 and $51 with intervening lows near $46. If you project the $9 head-to-neckline height below $46, the arithmetic target is $37. It is a projection that price need not reach.

Fidelity — technical indicators use historical observations; background, not evidence of a profitable pattern

What is Double Bottom?

Published by TradeHQ. Site creator and editorial approach: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date.

A double bottom is a W-shaped chart pattern with two troughs near a similar level. A later move above the intervening peak fits the pattern, but does not ensure that a rally continues.

DETAILED DEFINITION

The double bottom is a bullish reversal pattern that forms after a sustained downtrend, characterized by two consecutive troughs at approximately the same price level separated by a moderate peak (the neckline). The pattern resembles the letter 'W' on a chart and is commonly interpreted as a possible reversal near a repeated price low; the chart alone cannot establish that selling pressure has been exhausted. The conventional description records a sequence of price observations. The first bottom forms as the existing downtrend reaches a point where buyers emerge, creating a bounce. The subsequent rally creates the neckline — the intermediate peak between the two bottoms. However, the rally loses momentum and price declines again to retest the support level established by the first bottom. The second bottom is the critical test: if price rises again from the low, it records another bounce at that level without proving the cause or durability. Pattern confirmation occurs when price breaks above the neckline (the peak between the two bottoms). The measured move target equals the depth of the pattern — the distance from the bottoms to the neckline — projected upward from the neckline breakout point. Volume characteristics provide context but do not establish predictive reliability. Some descriptions compare volume during the two declines and the neckline break. Lower reported volume is an observation, not proof of reduced selling conviction or a future rebound. A volume observation does not establish a measured breakout failure rate. RSI divergence is another description of the selected historical data, not evidence of a dramatically higher success rate. If the RSI makes a higher low while price makes an equal or lower low at the second bottom, the oscillator records a smaller decline in its selected inputs; this does not validate a subsequent reversal.

KEY POINTS
W-shaped pattern with two tests of the same support level
Confirmed when price breaks above the neckline (middle peak)
RSI divergence is another historical observation, not independent proof of a profitable reversal
💡 WHY THIS MATTERS

Identify the two lows and the intervening high under fixed rules, including failed examples. A familiar pattern does not establish a beginner’s readiness or confidence level.

Worked exercise and its limits

Draw troughs near $30 separated by a $35 high. The $5 height gives a conventional projection of $40 after a break above $35, but the next move could reverse. State the tolerance used to call the troughs similar.

The Greeks — Delta, Gamma, Theta & Vega

The four Greeks quantify how an option's price reacts to stock moves, volatility, and the passage of time.

Contract worksheet only — no derivatives trading desk
This lesson teaches hypothetical options or futures contract mechanics. TradeHQ’s $100,000 virtual desk supports only its listed spot-style practice instruments; it cannot open, value, margin, exercise or settle an options or futures contract. Work through the contract calculations here rather than entering the example as a simulated order.
By Anuga Weerasinghe

Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.

QUICK ANSWER
The Greeks — Delta, Gamma, Theta & Vega

The four Greeks quantify how an option's price reacts to stock moves, volatility, and the passage of time. Delta estimates underlying-price sensitivity, not a guaranteed payoff or real-world event probability. Gamma is often relatively large near the strike close to expiration; volatility and other model inputs also matter.

Why Greeks matter

Greeks are model-based sensitivities to inputs, holding other inputs fixed. Delta describes underlying-price sensitivity; gamma describes a change in delta; theta describes time sensitivity; vega describes implied-volatility sensitivity. Interest rates and dividends can also matter. Finite market moves need not equal a first-order estimate, and different pricing models can produce different values.

Delta — directional exposure

A delta of 0.50 per share describes an approximate $0.50 option-price change for a $1 underlying move, with other inputs held fixed. For a 100-share contract that is about $50, before gamma and other effects. Some traders use delta as a rough probability shorthand, but it is not a calibrated real-world probability and need not match the model probability of finishing in the money.

Gamma — how fast delta changes

Gamma measures how delta changes as the underlying moves. It is often relatively large near the strike close to expiry, depending on volatility and other inputs. Dealer hedging can affect demand, but a chart or open-interest figure alone does not establish dealer positions, required hedges or the cause of a price move.

Theta — the ticking clock

Theta estimates an option value change as time passes under a model, holding other inputs fixed. State whether the quote is per share or per contract and whether a calendar or trading-day convention is used. Purchased options commonly have negative theta, but realised profit also depends on price, volatility and costs. Selling premium is not a guaranteed collection of that estimate.

Vega — volatility sensitivity

Vega estimates sensitivity to a one-percentage-point change in implied volatility, with other inputs held fixed. Implied volatility can change around earnings, but it need not rise before every release or fall afterwards. A long option can lose despite a favorable underlying move if time decay and a volatility decline offset that move.

Options have several model sensitivities: delta describes underlying-price sensitivity, gamma describes how delta changes with the underlying price, and theta and vega describe time and volatility sensitivities. Hold other model inputs fixed when interpreting each measure.

(Educational only — not financial advice. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Options contracts, Greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; the simulator does not execute them.)

KEY TAKEAWAYS
Delta estimates underlying-price sensitivity, not a guaranteed payoff or real-world event probability.
Gamma is often relatively large near the strike close to expiration; volatility and other model inputs also matter.
Theta is a model sensitivity; other price changes can offset or exceed it.
Vega measures volatility sensitivity; a change in implied volatility is a different quantity.

$0.10$0.30$0.50$0.90
3. 'IV crush' typically happens:
Right before earningsRight after earningsOn Fed decision dayAt market open
4. Which Greek measures the rate of change of delta?

Answer notes
What does theta measure? Options: Directional exposure; Time decay per day; Volatility sensitivity; Interest-rate risk. Correct answer: Time decay per day. Why: Theta is a model estimate of time sensitivity with other inputs held fixed; units and time conventions must be stated.
In the lesson example, a 0.50 delta and a $1 underlying rise imply approximately what change per option share, before other effects? Options: $0.10; $0.30; $0.50; $0.90. Correct answer: $0.50. Why: 0.50 × $1 = $0.50 per share, holding other inputs fixed; this is not an event probability.
'IV crush' typically happens: Options: Right before earnings; Right after earnings; On Fed decision day; At market open. Correct answer: Right after earnings. Why: A post-announcement drop in implied volatility is often called IV crush; it is not inevitable after every release.
Which Greek measures the rate of change of delta? Options: Vega; Theta; Gamma; Rho. Correct answer: Gamma. Why: Gamma tells you how quickly delta itself changes.

Options losses can be amplified by position size, leverage, volatility and time decay. This lesson measures those risks using hypothetical contract examples.

Contract worksheet only — no derivatives trading desk
This lesson teaches hypothetical options or futures contract mechanics. TradeHQ’s $100,000 virtual desk supports only its listed spot-style practice instruments; it cannot open, value, margin, exercise or settle an options or futures contract. By Anuga Weerasinghe

Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.

QUICK ANSWER
Options Risk Management — Sizing, Rolling & Cutting Losses

Options losses can be amplified by position size, leverage, volatility and time decay. This lesson measures those risks using hypothetical contract examples. Use a predefined practice risk budget and record the effect on drawdown. Model adverse scenarios for structures whose losses can exceed the premium collected.

Illustrative 1% budget for a defined-risk worksheet

For simulation, choose a small predefined risk budget before entering a position and compare how different limits affect drawdown. For example, 1% of a $100,000 practice account is $1,000. This is an educational parameter, not a universal real-money rule.

Testing a hypothetical loss multiplier

Naked puts and short strangles can create losses far larger than the premium collected. In a paper worksheet, model adverse moves explicitly and compare the resulting losses with a hypothetical risk budget rather than relying on one fixed multiplier. TradeHQ does not execute these option positions.

Rolling — extending, not doubling down

Rolling means closing an existing option and opening another with a different expiry and sometimes a different strike. A credit or debit alone does not determine whether the adjustment makes sense; compare the new maximum loss, break-even points, time remaining and total capital at risk in a worked example. Rolling options is not supported by TradeHQ's order engine.

When to cut a loss

Predefined exits can prevent open-ended decision-making, but no single percentage works for every option structure. In a worksheet with appropriate historical option prices, compare several hypothetical exit rules and record drawdown, average loss and opportunity cost. Account for execution assumptions and costs; TradeHQ's spot simulator cannot perform this options backtest.

Journaling every trade

For each hypothetical options example, record the thesis, dated volatility inputs, contract size, possible loss, exit assumptions and calculated P&L in a separate worksheet. TradeHQ's journal records supported simulator trades; it does not automatically capture options contracts or IV rank. Reviewing examples may reveal recurring mistakes, but no fixed number of trades establishes a reliable edge.

(Educational only — not financial advice. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Options contracts, Greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; the simulator does not execute them.)

KEY TAKEAWAYS
Use a predefined practice risk budget and record the effect on drawdown.
Model adverse scenarios for structures whose losses can exceed the premium collected.
Evaluate a roll by its full risk profile, not only by whether it creates a credit or debit.
Test predefined exits in simulation rather than treating one threshold as universal.

To guarantee profitTo define a planned exposure or loss assumptionTo predict volatilityTo avoid all drawdowns

Only whether it creates a creditOnly the new expiryThe new risk, break-even points, cost and time remainingNothing — rolling is always better
3. How can a hypothetical options exit rule be studied outside TradeHQ’s spot engine?
Assume one percentage always worksUse a separate options-data worksheet with explicit fills and costsChange the rule after every lossIgnore position size

Tax onlyReview recorded assumptions and mistakesRequired by regulatorsBoosts win rate automatically

Answer notes
Why define a risk budget before a simulated options trade? Options: To guarantee profit; To define a planned exposure or loss assumption; To predict volatility; To avoid all drawdowns. Correct answer: To define a planned exposure or loss assumption. Why: A risk budget records a planned exposure or loss assumption. It does not cap actual losses: gaps, execution, costs and contract obligations can produce a different result. No percentage fits every situation.
What should be compared when evaluating a roll? Options: Only whether it creates a credit; Only the new expiry; The new risk, break-even points, cost and time remaining; Nothing — rolling is always better. Correct answer: The new risk, break-even points, cost and time remaining. Why: A roll changes several dimensions of the position, so the full risk profile matters more than credit versus debit alone.
How can a hypothetical options exit rule be studied outside TradeHQ’s spot engine? Options: Assume one percentage always works; Use a separate options-data worksheet with explicit fills and costs; Change the rule after every loss; Ignore position size. Correct answer: Use a separate options-data worksheet with explicit fills and costs. Why: TradeHQ cannot execute an options backtest. A separate worksheet needs actual options observations and assumptions; a selected sample cannot validate future performance.
Why journal every trade? Options: Tax only; Review recorded assumptions and mistakes; Required by regulators; Boosts win rate automatically. Correct answer: Review recorded assumptions and mistakes. Why: A journal records assumptions and observed mistakes. It does not prove a statistical edge or predict future profits.

Contract worksheet only — no derivatives trading desk
This lesson teaches hypothetical options or futures contract mechanics. TradeHQ’s $100,000 virtual desk supports only its listed spot-style practice instruments; it cannot open, value, margin, exercise or settle an options or futures contract. Work through the contract calculations here rather than entering the example as a simulated order.
By Anuga Weerasinghe

Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.

QUICK ANSWER
Contango & Backwardation — Term Structure Explained

Compare prices across delivery dates and study carrying costs, supply conditions and the assumptions behind rolling exposure. Contango: later delivery trades above nearer delivery in the comparison; carrying costs can contribute. Backwardation: later delivery trades below nearer delivery; the curve alone does not establish a shortage.

Term structure — the futures curve

A futures curve compares quoted prices across the delivery dates available for a specified contract family and observation time. The number of listed expirations varies by product and exchange. Later delivery priced above nearer delivery is commonly called contango; the reverse comparison is backwardation. State which dates are being compared rather than assume the entire curve has one slope.

Why contango happens

Carrying costs such as storage, insurance and financing can contribute to higher prices for later delivery. A simplified example with $4 of carrying costs may illustrate that relationship, but convenience yield, constraints and market conditions also matter; there is no universal $4 premium or default curve.

Why backwardation happens

Backwardation means later-delivery contracts trade below nearer delivery in the comparison being made. Supply conditions and the value of immediate availability can contribute, but the curve alone does not prove a physical shortage or identify a future price direction.

The roll yield trap

A fund with futures exposure may replace expiring contracts according to its current published methodology. Rolling can affect performance relative to spot, alongside collateral returns, fees and the price path. A roll is not an automatic cash loss equal to the price gap; inspect the specific fund and observation period.

Trading implications

The curve records prices for different delivery dates. It is context for an educational comparison, not an automatic top, bottom or squeeze signal and not a direct measurement of commercial hedger positioning.

(Educational only — not financial advice. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Options contracts, Greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; the simulator does not execute them.)

KEY TAKEAWAYS
Contango: later delivery trades above nearer delivery in the comparison; carrying costs can contribute.
Backwardation: later delivery trades below nearer delivery; the curve alone does not establish a shortage.
Futures-fund returns depend on methodology, contract price changes, collateral returns and costs.
The curve shows delivery prices, not the identity or positioning of participants.

1. Further-dated below front month =
ContangoBackwardationEquilibriumRollover
2. Which factor can make a futures fund differ from spot performance?
Guaranteed gainsContract selection and rolling methodologyNo costsIdentical exposure
3. Which factor can contribute to contango in a storable-commodity example?
A guaranteed shortageCarrying costsThe ticker symbol aloneA universal price rule
4. Which condition can contribute to backwardation, without being proven by the curve alone?
Quiet marketPhysical shortageDelistingLow vol
Submit & complete lesson
Answer notes
Further-dated below front month = Options: Contango; Backwardation; Equilibrium; Rollover. Correct answer: Backwardation. Why: Backwardation describes relative delivery prices; it does not by itself prove a shortage.
Which factor can make a futures fund differ from spot performance? Options: Guaranteed gains; Contract selection and rolling methodology; No costs; Identical exposure. Correct answer: Contract selection and rolling methodology. Why: Methodology, contract price changes, collateral returns and costs affect fund performance.
Which factor can contribute to contango in a storable-commodity example? Options: A guaranteed shortage; Carrying costs; The ticker symbol alone; A universal price rule. Correct answer: Carrying costs. Why: Carrying costs can contribute to higher deferred futures prices. Convenience yield and other conditions can offset those costs; storable commodities are not always in contango.
Which condition can contribute to backwardation, without being proven by the curve alone? Options: Quiet market; Physical shortage; Delisting; Low vol. Correct answer: Physical shortage. Why: Immediate demand for physical supply and convenience yield can contribute to backwardation. The curve alone does not prove a shortage or identify participants’ motives.

Reading CPI and Inflation Data

CPI measures selected consumer-price changes. Read the release, its definitions and components without assuming a predictable market response. Use the current BLS release calendar; releases are generally scheduled at 8:30 AM Eastern. Core CPI excludes food and energy; the FOMC’s longer-run inflation target uses PCE.

What CPI actually measures

The Consumer Price Index is a monthly Bureau of Labor Statistics survey of prices paid by urban consumers for a basket of goods and services. It has two headline flavours: headline CPI (includes food and energy) and core CPI (excludes them, because they're volatile). Core readings are used to study trends, while the FOMC states its longer-run 2% inflation goal in terms of the annual change in the PCE price index.

The release mechanics

Check the current BLS release calendar for CPI timing; scheduled releases are generally at 8:30 AM Eastern. Market reactions depend on expectations and other information. No fixed first-minute percentage move or single class of participant is established by this lesson.

Consensus, surprise and market reaction

A consensus figure is an aggregation of a particular survey’s forecasts, not the view of every economist. Record the provider, collection time and aggregation method before comparing it with the release. The difference is often called a surprise, but its sign alone cannot determine yields, exchange rates or share returns; expectations, revisions and other information can also matter.

The three-layer read

For a study worksheet, compare the reported headline and core changes with a specifically identified expectation, then inspect the component contributions and measurement period. Headline and core answer different questions. The Fed’s stated longer-run target uses PCE inflation rather than either CPI measure, and policy considers more than one statistic.

(Educational only — not financial advice. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Options contracts, Greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; the simulator does not execute them.)

KEY TAKEAWAYS
Use the current BLS release calendar; releases are generally scheduled at 8:30 AM Eastern.
Core CPI excludes food and energy; the FOMC’s longer-run inflation target uses PCE.
A release-versus-survey difference is context, not a deterministic market signal.
Read the underlying components.

Answer notes
The Fed's 2% longer-run inflation goal is measured using: Options: Headline CPI; Core CPI; PCE price index; PPI. Correct answer: PCE price index. Why: The FOMC states its 2% longer-run inflation goal in terms of the annual change in the PCE price index.
CPI is released at: Options: 8:00 AM ET; 8:30 AM ET; 10:00 AM ET; 2:00 PM ET. Correct answer: 8:30 AM ET. Why: 8:30 AM Eastern.
What distinguishes core CPI from headline CPI? Options: Core is always higher; Core excludes food and energy; Headline CPI is not reported; Core predicts future inflation. Correct answer: Core excludes food and energy. Why: Core CPI excludes food and energy, whose prices can be volatile. It offers one view of underlying inflation; headline CPI covers the full specified basket. Neither series alone establishes future inflation.
A CPI result above one survey’s median forecast establishes: Options: The next stock return; A difference from that specified forecast; A guaranteed rate increase; Which participant moved the market. Correct answer: A difference from that specified forecast. Why: A forecast difference alone does not identify market participants or determine the next price move.

Learn Trading in the Philippines

TradeHQ provides a free paper-trading environment for people in the Philippines who want to learn how US and global markets work without risking money. Real-money provider eligibility and rules should be checked against current official sources.

Educational simulation only — not financial advice.

QUICK ANSWER
Is TradeHQ suitable for learners in the Philippines?

Yes. TradeHQ is a free educational trading simulator accessible from the Philippines with no required signup or payment. TradeHQ is a virtual practice tool, not a broker, and does not execute real trades. This page does not determine your legal eligibility or a provider’s regulatory status. Every account starts with $100,000 in virtual cash for an educational worksheet; access does not establish eligibility for a real account. Educational simulation only — not financial advice.

Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. Regulatory source check: 2026-10-18.

Linked regulator or registry information; no verification of individual eligibility, tax rates or remittance permission. No professional legal or financial review.

Philippine SEC — eRAMP capital-market participants
LOCAL REGULATOR
Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC Philippines)

Check current local rules and provider registration with the relevant official authority. This guide does not certify regulatory compliance.

LOCAL EXCHANGE

Philippine Stock Exchange (PSE)

Local currency: PHP

Why practise before you fund a real account

Paper trading lets you learn market mechanics without opening or funding a real-money brokerage account. If you later consider real trading, verify the current requirements with the Philippine SEC, the exchange and the provider involved.

How market access actually works in the Philippines

For real-money market access, check the Philippine SEC's current registry of capital-market participants and the provider's current terms. TradeHQ does not state that a particular bank setup, overseas platform, fractional product or account route is available to every resident. Nothing on TradeHQ requires a brokerage account or payment.

How much capital do you really need?

TradeHQ does not publish a real-money starting amount because provider minimums, fees and personal circumstances vary. Use the simulator to learn the mechanics first, and verify any current account minimum or fee directly with a regulated provider.

What to follow from the Philippines
The PSEi as the headline measure of local equity sentiment
USD/PHP, which matters to any household receiving remittances
The PSE’s dated index constituent and weight disclosures, rather than an assumed permanent sector ranking
US company reports as external research examples; virtual availability does not establish real-market access
Country-specific practice worksheet

Optional study worksheet: assume a fictional USD 100 remittance and choose two hypothetical PHP-per-USD rates. Calculate the peso receipt under each before fees. Then add an explicit fee assumption and compare the net receipts. This separates currency translation and transaction costs from an investment return. It does not forecast USD/PHP or establish a bank or brokerage route. Select a study schedule that fits school or work rather than following a foreign market overnight.

Educational simulation only — not financial, tax or legal advice. Confirm all local rules with a licensed professional in the Philippines.

Students and beginners can use the simulator and courses to practise market concepts and keep a record of simulated decisions without using real money.

Broker/dealers and other capital-market participants listed in the Philippine SEC's current eRAMP registry

Tax treatment depends on current law, the product and individual circumstances. Check current official Philippine guidance or a qualified tax professional; TradeHQ does not provide tax advice.

rows.text:
Privacy Policy

This policy describes the data flows used by the current TradeHQ website, including optional analytics and advertising.

Last Updated: November 8, 2026

Privacy at a Glance
✓
Core simulator features can be used without creating an account.
✓
Guest portfolios stay in your browser; account cash, positions and server-recorded trades restore from Supabase.
✓
Optional accounts and community features can store data with Supabase.
✓
Optional Arena and leaderboard-to-registration analytics require fresh adult opt-in; session replay and automatic interaction capture are disabled. Google advertising has separate privacy choices.
✓
No real-money deposit or brokerage account is required for simulated trading.
Information TradeHQ Handles
TradeHQ can be used without creating an account. The data handled depends on the features you choose.

• Guest simulator data: practice cash, positions and trade history are stored in your browser with a separate browser-local recovery copy. You can download or explicitly restore a portable practice backup JSON file containing trading history and any private journal notes. The backup feature does not upload this file. Backup formats can be manually edited: TradeHQ validates file structure and arithmetic but does not certify authenticity, investment performance or leaderboard ranking. An imported guest file remains unverified. Guest learning-journey progress, course progress, streaks and related settings remain browser-stored. For signed-in users, lesson completion, unfinished quiz answers, reading position and first-trade journey progress may also be saved privately in Supabase and synchronized across devices when online. New beginner-journey reflection text stays on the device. Older reflections already synchronized remain private in the account. Streaks and unrelated browser preferences are not part of this account sync.
• Signed-in portfolio data: Supabase stores account cash, positions and server-recorded practice orders, including asset, quantity, execution price, fees, time and simulated result. These account records restore across devices when the service is available. Signed-in users can also download a server-signed current-cycle historical practice export and verify its integrity against their authenticated account. This file may contain account identifiers and private transaction details; it is not publicly shared or accepted as an upload that replaces ranked trades. A first-time browser import stores cash and positions as an unranked portfolio; earlier guest trade history stays in its original browser. Starting a fresh ranked practice cycle archives the previous account snapshot privately. Journals remain browser-held; signed-in lesson and beginner-journey progress can sync privately and are not used to determine public trading ranks.
• Optional account data: if you create an account, Supabase processes authentication data such as your email or provider identity and can store profile fields including username, country and bio.
• Community data: signed-in features can store selected practice statistics, public-profile settings, reviews and duel/challenge records. A separate setting, OFF by default, lets a member voluntarily disclose up to 20 current-cycle server-recorded simulated trade entries on an otherwise public profile: asset, buy/sell, quantity, execution price, fee and date. Private journals, reflections, past cycles and browser-only records are never shared by this feature. These are simulated results, not brokerage statements or verified real-money performance.
• Review interactions: likes are stored with your account ID and the review ID to enforce one like per account. Public pages show totals, not individual liker identities. Owner replies are public. Reviews removed from public view remain in the private admin panel for restoration.
• Optional TradeHQ Newsletter: if you explicitly request the educational newsletter, TradeHQ stores your email address, consent/confirmation status, the date and source of signup, unsubscribe status, and delivery receipts in private Supabase records. Resend handles email delivery and receives your address for confirmations and issues. We never add prior contact records to the mailing list without permission. Every newsletter provides an unsubscribe link, and you may use the contact page to request deletion.
• Contact messages: by default the contact page opens your email app or lets you copy a draft into webmail. If the optional direct-send service is configured, Cloudflare Turnstile processes challenge and connection information and Resend processes the message, sender reply address and recipient information to deliver it to the maintainer's inbox. TradeHQ does not retain direct-send message bodies in its application database. The maintainer's email provider retains delivered messages according to its settings.
• Technical data: hosting, authentication, security and abuse-prevention services can receive normal request information such as IP address, browser/device information and server logs.
• Optional analytics and advertising data: TradeHQ offers a newly scoped analytics choice only to visitors affirmatively confirming they are at least 18. This confirmation is for optional analytics; it is not an age restriction on lessons, guest practice or sign-in. Visitors under 18 should reject optional analytics. If accepted, Amplitude can receive limited Practice Arena milestone events and two leaderboard registration-flow events (an eligible signed-out leaderboard visit, and a newly created account subsequently authenticated in that same browser within seven days), along with its pseudonymous browser identity and ordinary network metadata. The two leaderboard custom events contain no email, account ID, username, profile details, portfolio data, transaction information, or form content. The temporary seven-day same-browser attribution marker stores only a visit timestamp and is cleared on consent rejection or successful attribution. No custom tracking occurs when analytics is declined; the website does not claim visitor identity is anonymous. Automatic page, click, form, network and attribution collection and session replay are disabled; the two explicitly triggered attribution events are the only leaderboard funnel measurement. Earlier v1/v2 analytics permissions are not reused. Google AdSense has separate advertising choices and may use cookies or similar identifiers for ad delivery, measurement and, where applicable, personalisation.
• Practice Arena research: exercise decisions, private written reasons, closing reflections and history stay in your browser and are not automatically submitted to a research database. An optional, adult-only research questionnaire keeps answers on the open page and only prepares an email if you deliberately choose to do so; you must send that email yourself. Sending an email reveals your sender address and may include other email-provider metadata. Answers are not anonymous once linked with a sender or identifying comments. If you accept Amplitude analytics, TradeHQ may record Arena view/start/finish/resume milestones, scenario ID and difficulty, and whether this browser returned on a later day. Custom Arena events do not include trading choices, portfolio values, account IDs, written notes or questionnaire answers. This opt-in measurement uses the existing Amplitude service's consented visitor identity; it does not create a separate TradeHQ research identifier. Declining analytics disables those custom milestones. A same-browser return event does not prove a person learned or voluntarily returned.

TradeHQ does not require a payment card, bank account or brokerage account to place simulated trades.
How Information Is Used
TradeHQ uses data only for the feature that needs it: operating the simulator, authenticating optional accounts, showing profile/community features, preventing abuse, responding to messages, delivering a voluntarily confirmed TradeHQ Newsletter subscription, diagnosing problems and improving the service.

Amplitude is used for limited, explicitly triggered Arena and leaderboard-to-new-account registration analytics after renewed adult opt-in. TradeHQ measures only consenting eligible visitors and same-browser new-account confirmations within seven days; email-link confirmations in another browser and visitors who reject analytics are not included, so any conversion rate is an incomplete proxy, not a claim about all visitors. This site's Amplitude configuration disables session replay, automatic page and click capture, form interactions, network tracking and remote automatic-enablement settings. We do not claim that disabling those features makes Amplitude's pseudonymous identifiers or request metadata anonymous.

Ad-serving scripts and placements are currently disabled on TradeHQ, including newly published courses, account pages and error screens. The publisher verification meta tag and ads.txt do not enable ad serving. Before advertising can be enabled, TradeHQ must verify Google site approval, suitable reviewed inventory, placement controls and applicable consent configuration. If advertising is enabled, Google and its partners may place or read cookies and use similar technologies, web beacons, IP addresses and other identifiers to deliver and measure ads. Third parties may collect information as a result of ad serving. Advertising cookies can reflect prior visits to TradeHQ or other sites and, where consent and law permit, support personalised ads. These uses remain subject to the applicable privacy choices. Advertising may be personalized, non-personalized or limited depending on consent, location and Google settings.

TradeHQ does not sell simulated portfolio data to brokers or financial institutions and does not execute real-money trades.
Storage, Visibility & Retention
Browser data remains on the device until the browser, the user or TradeHQ's own reset controls remove it. Clearing all site data also removes browser-local recovery copies; download a portfolio backup to preserve it separately. Clearing browser data removes local records; it does not delete a signed-in portfolio already stored in Supabase.

Optional account and community data can be stored by Supabase for as long as the related account or feature requires it. Newsletter consent records and delivery receipts are retained while relevant to operating the requested subscription, unsubscribe suppression, and compliance; contact TradeHQ to request deletion or information. New accounts start with a private profile. You may explicitly make your profile public later; only then can chosen profile fields and selected simulated statistics appear on public pages. Existing members retain their chosen visibility, and public trade-history sharing remains a separate off-by-default permission.

Scored educational trophy challenges are optional for registered users. TradeHQ stores the minimal account-linked challenge ID, source version, pass/miss and score receipt, and the resulting permanent trophy ID and issue date. It does not store the answer choices you selected, your written Arena notes or a copy of each Daily case in the trophy award record. Existing device-only learning progress is not used to create server-verified public awards. Account deletion removes the separate trophy records.

Trophy display is disabled by default even for a public trader profile, including older profiles that were historically public by default. After an account is confirmed and its profile is deliberately public, the owner may separately enable display of one earned trophy flair and up to three earned pinned trophies. Only the chosen trophy names/icons are shown publicly; scores, assessment dates, balances, trades, contacts and private learning history are not included. You may withdraw this permission in My Trophy Cabinet, or hide the entire profile; both actions stop the optional trophy display.

The optional leaderboard attribution marker contains only a local visit timestamp and is eligible for matching for no more than seven days. If the person does not return, the expired timestamp may remain in browser storage until the next relevant page access, consent withdrawal or site-data clearing; it is then discarded or replaced. A successful attributed registration also clears the marker. Analytics and advertising data at external providers are retained according to their settings and policies; TradeHQ does not state a fixed provider retention period where it cannot verify one.

TradeHQ uses hosted infrastructure and access controls intended to protect stored data, but no online service can guarantee absolute security.
Age and Optional Features
The core simulator works without an account. The optional account flow does not ask for age, so TradeHQ does not determine a visitor's age from that form.

Public profiles and community features can publish the information and simulated statistics you choose to share. Avoid including private or sensitive information in public fields. A parent or guardian can use the contact page to raise a privacy concern involving a young user. Optional Amplitude Arena and leaderboard registration-flow analytics are unavailable unless the visitor confirms they are at least 18 and affirmatively accepts the updated permission. This declaration is not verified age assurance and does not resolve every jurisdiction's child-safety requirements. Visitors under 18 should reject analytics; the core simulator remains available.

An advertising consent choice alone does not determine age or replace age-specific advertising protections where they apply.
Service Providers, Cookies & Your Choices
TradeHQ relies on third parties including Cloudflare Pages for hosting, Supabase for optional authentication/database features, Resend for explicitly requested newsletter emails and contact messages, Amplitude for optional adult-consented Arena and leaderboard-to-registration analytics without session replay, and, if advertising is enabled in a future reviewed release, Google AdSense for consented advertising. These providers can process data in countries other than your own under their own legal and contractual arrangements.

Optional Amplitude scripts are blocked unless a visitor expressly confirms they are at least 18 and accepts the newly expanded analytics choice. Prior v1 and v2 choices are not carried forward. Accepting stores a pseudonymous Amplitude browser identifier locally to support consented Arena measurement and the limited same-browser leaderboard registration funnel. You can reject analytics or withdraw a previous choice from this privacy page; withdrawal stops new custom events but does not automatically erase historical events already held by a provider. Contact TradeHQ for a privacy or deletion request. Analytics acceptance does not grant advertising consent.

Before any future advertising release, TradeHQ must verify the applicable Google-certified consent-management configuration for regional advertising choices in the EEA, United Kingdom and Switzerland. Availability of the published message depends on Google's configuration and the visitor's region; an unavailable message does not constitute consent. The Google message lets you consent, decline or manage individual options. When it applies, use Advertising privacy choices on this page or in the footer to change or withdraw your decision.

In supported US states, Google's Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information link lets you opt out of the sale or sharing of personal information for advertising. Google applies restricted data processing to applicable opt-out requests. These regional messages manage Google's advertising partners; optional Amplitude analytics are controlled separately.

You can also clear browser storage/cookies, use browser privacy controls and manage ad personalization through Google Ads Settings. When the Google message is available, its partner list describes the vendors and purposes covered by your advertising choices.

Depending on where you live, privacy law may give you rights to access, correct, delete, restrict or object to certain processing. Use the TradeHQ contact page for a privacy request. The exact rights available depend on your jurisdiction.

Optional Arena and leaderboard new-account registration analytics use a pseudonymous browser identifier only after renewed consent from a visitor confirming they are at least 18; no account ID, email or portfolio is included in the custom funnel events. The 18+ confirmation is for optional analytics; it is not an age restriction on lessons, guest practice or sign-in. Visitors under 18 should reject optional analytics. Diversification Strategies
Position Sizing & The 2% Rule

Illustration for position sizing & the 2% rule.

Position sizing converts chosen assumptions into an exposure. The often-mentioned 2% rule is a heuristic, not an appropriate loss limit for every person or trade. A planned exit can be missed, and losses can exceed the worksheet assumption.

💡
Example

Choose a hypothetical $100,000 account and a 2% planned loss amount: $100,000 × 0.02 = $2,000. With an assumed $100 entry and $95 exit, the $5 difference gives $2,000 ÷ $5 = 400 shares and $40,000 purchase notional before fees. This quantity is a calculation, not a recommendation.

Specify entry, assumed exit, available cash, units and transaction costs.
Check affordability separately: a worksheet quantity is not automatically an executable order.
Repeat with a worse fill: 400 shares sold at $90 lose $4,000 before costs, twice the planned amount.
Include existing positions when evaluating total exposure; a per-trade number does not cap portfolio losses.
Pro Tip

TradeHQ supports market orders. Keep the hypothetical exit in a journal and compare it with the practice result; writing a stop price does not place a protective stop order.

Candlestick Patterns

Moving Averages (SMA & EMA)
RSI & MACD Indicators
Candlestick Patterns

Illustration for candlestick patterns.

Illustration for candlestick patterns.

Candlesticks summarize open, high, low and close over a stated interval. Common green-up coloring means close above open; the configured colors must be checked. Shape names describe historical observations, not validated forecasts by themselves.

💡
Example

Open 100, high 105, low 99 and close 103 give a body of 3, upper wick of 2, lower wick of 1 and total range of 6. Close 99 instead would describe a down body of 1 using the same open; the shape changes with the actual data.

Doji: open and close are close relative to a chosen tolerance and interval.
Hammer: commonly a small body near the upper end with a longer lower wick; definitions vary.
Engulfing: a multi-candle body comparison, so check whether a definition uses bodies or the full high-low range.
Pro Tip

Label the symbol, source, interval and definition before identifying a shape. Finding a named pattern after a price move does not establish that it could predict the move in advance.

Short-term vs Long-term Strategies

Illustration for short-term vs long-term strategies.

Holding period is one part of a strategy description. Intraday trading generally opens and closes within a session, while swing and longer-term approaches retain exposure across sessions. The labels alone do not define a reliable return, suitable workload or tax outcome.

Compare the time needed to observe and record decisions under each hypothetical approach.
More transactions can increase costs; actual fees and turnover must be measured rather than assumed from a label.
Holding overnight adds exposure to news and gaps. Holding longer does not ensure recovery or eliminate permanent loss.
Tax treatment depends on jurisdiction, product and account; no universal long-term tax advantage is asserted here.
💡
Example

Invented comparison: two approaches each begin at $1,000 and end at $1,020 before costs. If one completes 20 round trips costing $2 each, its ending value is $980; two such round trips leave $1,016. This isolates cost arithmetic and does not establish that either approach could earn the assumed gross result.

Pro Tip

Choose a practice review task, such as comparing planned and observed costs over a fixed period. No number of study hours or selected profitable months certifies readiness for real-money trading.

Asset allocation describes how value is divided among exposures. Its effect depends on holdings, correlations and the period examined; it does not guarantee performance or universally outrank every other decision.

Age alone cannot determine a suitable allocation. Objectives, liabilities, time horizon and ability to bear loss also matter; a simulator cannot make that determination.

The 100-Minus-Age Rule

The 100-minus-age shortcut is a simplified heuristic, not a suitability assessment:

Subtract your age from 100 = % in stocks
Age 25: 75% stocks, 25% bonds/cash
Age 50: 50% stocks, 50% bonds/cash
Age 70: 30% stocks, 70% bonds/cash
This shortcut ignores liabilities, product risks and ability to bear losses; it cannot establish suitability.

Setting Up Your Bitcoin Simulator Environment

Learn how virtual cash, provider price snapshots and simulated order limitations work in TradeHQ. TradeHQ balances and Bitcoin holdings are virtual, not withdrawable funds or actual cryptocurrency. Price sources and observation timestamps matter; a practice quote is not an executable live market order.

Initializing the Virtual Balance

When you first access a trading simulator, the platform typically provisions a fixed amount of virtual capital to enable practice without committing real funds. This starting balance serves as your primary accounting ledger for all subsequent buy and sell transactions across supported spot assets. Users must recognize that this currency holds no real-world monetary value and cannot be withdrawn or converted into fiat money under any circumstances. Understanding this foundational boundary ensures you treat the simulation strictly as an educational sandbox rather than a speculative wealth-generation tool.

Virtual practice avoids real-money exposure and can help a learner inspect order mechanics and assumptions. It does not reproduce every emotional or financial constraint of a real account. Record what the exercise tested and its limitations rather than treating a practice habit as evidence of future trading ability.

Understanding snapshot price data

TradeHQ's displayed Bitcoin quote is a practice valuation input, not a live executable offer. Supported instruments may use periodically refreshed provider observations, while unsupported ones can use fixed simulator prices. Data providers may aggregate venue observations under documented methodologies, but the displayed price is not necessarily a global index or a price at which any quantity could trade. When comparing two values, first check the asset identifier, source and observation timestamps. This distinction helps prevent the assumption that a recent browser refresh means the price is current, liquid or executable on a real exchange.

Provider observations can be delayed, cached, unavailable or updated at different intervals depending on the instrument and service. An API call that succeeds does not prove its underlying data is fresh, and a missing quote must not be treated as a zero price. For an educational worksheet, record the time of the observed Bitcoin reference and the time TradeHQ fetched it, if both are available. Compare snapshots only after matching units and quote currencies. This process highlights data limitations and does not reproduce the trades, order book or transaction costs of a real venue.

Understanding Spot Execution Limits

TradeHQ provides virtual cash alongside straightforward market buy and sell orders for spot assets including cryptocurrencies and stocks. Crucially, the platform does not support advanced financial instruments such as short selling, limit orders, leveraged positions, futures, or options. This intentional constraint simplifies the user experience, allowing beginners to focus entirely on basic asset accumulation and portfolio tracking. Understanding these structural boundaries prevents unrealistic expectations regarding available order types during your practice sessions.

For a worksheet, start with $100,000 virtual cash and suppose Bitcoin has a hypothetical displayed price of $40,000. Buying 2 virtual units costs $80,000 before fees. TradeHQ adds a 0.1% virtual purchase fee of $80, leaving $19,920 cash; the recorded position is worth $80,000 at the same assumed quote, for $99,920 marked equity. At a later invented quote of $41,000, the 2-unit position would be marked at $82,000 and total equity at $101,920. These are not real fills, guaranteed prices or a forecast. Record source timestamps and any rounding.

Establishing Personal Evaluation Metrics

Evaluating your simulator performance requires establishing clear benchmarks before executing your very first virtual trade order. Rather than focusing solely on raw portfolio growth, you should track metrics such as trade frequency, asset allocation balance, and drawdown depth. Documenting your strategic rationale for each simulated purchase creates a reliable historical record for subsequent performance reviews. This structured approach transforms casual experimentation into a rigorous, repeatable educational process.

Before the first virtual purchase, write down a clear learning goal such as calculating the purchase fee, reading the source timestamp or finding remaining virtual cash. Compare the intended notional with the recorded quantity and inspect any discrepancy rather than attributing a profit to skill. Repeat the same calculation under a falling Bitcoin-price scenario and record how a 0.1% sale fee changes the outcome. A practice log can expose arithmetic mistakes and uncertain assumptions but does not demonstrate that a trading strategy works in real markets or guarantees a measurable psychological benefit.

KEY TAKEAWAYS
TradeHQ balances and Bitcoin holdings are virtual, not withdrawable funds or actual cryptocurrency.
Price sources and observation timestamps matter; a practice quote is not an executable live market order.
The simulator applies 0.1% virtual fees to buy and sale notionals, affecting remaining cash and account equity.

QUICK ANSWER
Executing Spot Trades in the Simulator

Learn step-by-step mechanics for placing market buy and sell orders within a virtual spot portfolio. TradeHQ's spot holdings represent fictional positions rather than direct legal ownership of Bitcoin. Every buy and sale changes the virtual cash ledger by the order notional and a 0.1% virtual fee.

Placing Your First Market Buy Order

To place a virtual Bitcoin market purchase, select the supported instrument and enter the intended amount. TradeHQ records the simulated transaction using its displayed practice price input, not a real exchange's executable bid or ask. The virtual cash debit includes both the purchase notional and a 0.1% simulator transaction fee. A successful simulated order increases fictional Bitcoin exposure in the account ledger rather than transferring ownership of an on-chain token. Review the recorded quantity, cash and price source after submission. These calculations are educational and cannot establish actual exchange fill quality.

As a hypothetical first-trade calculation, assume a fresh TradeHQ practice account has $100,000 virtual cash and a Bitcoin snapshot price of $50,000. Buying 0.1 virtual BTC has a $5,000 notional value; the 0.1% buy fee is $5. The simulated account would record 0.1 virtual BTC and $94,995 remaining cash, so equity at the same practice quote is $99,995. This is not actual Bitcoin ownership or an executable market offer. Compare the calculated result with the recorded ledger and check the quote's source and observation time before interpreting any difference.

Managing Spot Asset Holdings

Once your spot purchase settles, the acquired asset remains in your portfolio until you decide to execute a corresponding sale. Unlike derivative contracts, spot holdings represent a simulated token position in a virtual ledger within the context of the simulation environment. You must monitor how market price fluctuations impact the total valuation of your holdings over successive trading sessions. This ongoing observation helps you understand the direct relationship between asset quantity and aggregate portfolio worth.

A price change can alter portfolio weights. Rebalancing is one possible worksheet rule: compare it with leaving weights unchanged under the same price path, costs and chosen targets. Neither approach is universally required or guarantees a successful portfolio.

Executing Market Sell Orders

A virtual market sale reduces the recorded Bitcoin quantity and adds net proceeds to the remaining practice cash balance after a 0.1% sale fee. The simulator uses its displayed practice input, not an order-book fill from a real venue. A sale may be used to practise reconciling cash and positions, calculating a gain or loss, or comparing hypothetical outcomes under different prices. The calculation does not prove that comparable real liquidity would be available or that an actual sale would execute instantly. Keep virtual accounting and real market execution as different questions.

When preparing an exit worksheet, state the objective: for example, learning fee accounting or comparing position values under two possible price paths. A price decline alone does not mean that a sale is objectively required, and a price increase does not guarantee a better future outcome. TradeHQ does not execute conditional stop-loss or limit orders, so the learner must not assume that an exit can be scheduled at a precise price. Compare the hypothetical choice to hold against the hypothetical choice to sell after costs, and describe the uncertainty rather than prescribing a strategy.

Handling Execution Reality and Limitations

TradeHQ simplifies actual market execution. Its market orders use a displayed practice input, and each virtual buy and sale charges a 0.1% fee. The simulator does not model order-book depth, queue priority, partial fills or calibrated slippage. For a second worksheet, selling 0.1 BTC at an assumed $51,000 produces $5,100 notional less a $5.10 sale fee, or $5,094.90 proceeds. Subtracting the original $5,005 acquisition cost gives an illustrative $89.90 gain. A $49,000 sale instead gives $4,895.10 proceeds and a $109.90 loss; neither scenario predicts market outcomes.

Simulated environments cannot replicate the psychological pressure of managing real capital during extreme market volatility and sudden downturns. While you can practice the mechanical steps of buying and selling, the emotional stakes remain entirely artificial throughout the process. Acknowledging this psychological gap helps keep your educational progress in proper perspective as you refine your analytical skills. Use the simulator to master mechanics, not as a definitive test of emotional resilience.

KEY TAKEAWAYS
TradeHQ's spot holdings represent fictional positions rather than direct legal ownership of Bitcoin.
Every buy and sale changes the virtual cash ledger by the order notional and a 0.1% virtual fee.
Simplified simulated fills do not reproduce exchange liquidity, slippage or emotional stakes.

Evaluating Performance and Managing Drawdowns

Analyze virtual trading results, calculate portfolio drawdowns, and evaluate the assumptions behind a hypothetical approach based on objective data. Total virtual equity includes cash and all marked holdings, net of simulated fees. Drawdown is measured from an observed peak; it is not the same as return from starting equity.

Analyzing Portfolio Valuation and Returns

Evaluating your simulator performance requires calculating the percentage change between your initial capital and current portfolio value. This calculation must account for both uninvested virtual cash and the fluctuating market value of your active spot holdings. Recomputing your total portfolio value after every major price move ensures your performance metrics remain accurate and up to date. Regular valuation checks prevent small calculation errors from compounding into misleading performance reports over time.

When reviewing your returns, separate broad market trends from the specific impact of your asset allocation decisions. If the entire digital asset market rises, your portfolio may show a profit even if your individual selections underperformed. Conversely, a declining market can produce negative returns despite sound portfolio structuring and disciplined position sizing. Learning to isolate your personal execution quality from macroeconomic tailwinds is essential for honest self-assessment.

Understanding Drawdown in Trading

A drawdown measures the decline from an earlier portfolio peak to a later marked value, expressed relative to that peak. In a hypothetical example, virtual equity reaches $110,000 and later falls to $88,000. The $22,000 decline divided by $110,000 equals 20% drawdown. If the starting equity was $100,000, however, the ending $88,000 represents a 12% total loss from the start. Drawdown and starting-balance return use different denominators. These are invented marked values, not evidence of actual fills, emotional tolerance or worst-case future loss.

A calculated historical drawdown describes only the measured price and account-value observations. It does not establish the largest future loss, the probability of recovery or how a particular person will respond emotionally to an actual investment loss. In a snapshot-based simulator, unobserved highs and lows may also be absent from the marked-equity series. For a more useful exercise, compare the selected path with an alternative declining or recovering path and document the number of observations, their timestamps and the effect of 0.1% transaction fees. These are educational comparisons, not performance forecasts.

Conducting Structured Practice Reviews

A periodic virtual-trade review can document the learner's assumptions, recorded transactions, fees and marked portfolio values. It does not prove that subjective bias has disappeared or that the same decision would succeed when real savings are at risk. For each hypothetical transaction, record the source timestamp, price input, virtual quantity, reason for the order and the outcome measured on the simulator's ledger. Compare these observations with a stated plan and note what remains unknown, including alternative market outcomes and unmodelled order-book effects. This is a record-keeping exercise rather than financial advice.

Try a three-observation worksheet for the same hypothetical account: $100,000 at the start, $110,000 at a later observed peak, and $88,000 at the end. Calculate the −12% starting-balance return and 20% peak-to-end drawdown. Then compare a different ending value of $121,000 and explain why sampled observations cannot reveal all intraperiod moves. Include remaining virtual cash and any transaction fees in the account totals. Write down which facts were calculated and which conclusions remain unsupported, particularly regarding real-market profitability and skill.

Honest Limitations of Simulation Practice

A simulator can explain market-order accounting and portfolio mathematics, but it does not fully reproduce real-money financial risk, psychological pressure or exchange execution conditions. TradeHQ models a 0.1% virtual fee on each buy and sale; it does not model the full order book, queue priority or calibrated slippage. Quotes can be delayed snapshots or fixed educational values, rather than reliable offers to buy or sell. Do not infer real-world trading competence, personal financial suitability or expected future profit from a virtual completion badge or a profitable practice sequence.

Simulator models do not reproduce every execution, liquidity or custody condition. State the source and observation time of a price input and distinguish an aggregate reference from an available execution quote. A completed lesson or favorable simulated result does not certify trading competence.

KEY TAKEAWAYS
Total virtual equity includes cash and all marked holdings, net of simulated fees.
Drawdown is measured from an observed peak; it is not the same as return from starting equity.
A review can document decisions but cannot eliminate bias, prove skill or forecast real-market outcomes.

Managing Concentration Risk and Portfolio Drift

Understand how concentration risk builds up and how price changes cause your portfolio to drift from its targets.

Prepared with AI assistance · Publication review recorded by Anuga Weerasinghe · 09/10/2026
QUICK ANSWER
Managing Concentration Risk and Portfolio Drift

Understand how concentration risk builds up and how price changes cause your portfolio to drift from its targets. Concentration risk leaves a portfolio highly vulnerable to negative shocks in a single asset or sector. Portfolio drift occurs naturally as market price movements change the relative weights of your assets over time.

Understanding Concentration Risk

Concentration describes exposure to a holding, sector or shared risk factor. If 80% of a hypothetical portfolio is in one token and it falls 50% with all other values unchanged, the portfolio falls 40% before costs. An adverse announcement need not produce that particular price move. Several holdings can remain exposed to the same shock, so diversification is a question about exposures as well as asset count. This example illustrates sensitivity rather than prescribing a maximum weight.

A learner can choose an exposure limit to test as an explicit classroom assumption. Ten percent in one holding is one possible input, not a universal professional standard or a boundary between acceptable and unacceptable investments. Compare more than one threshold, including how turnover, costs and shared exposures change. A journal can record why a hypothetical limit was chosen and when it was reviewed; the rule does not prevent bias or prove positive investment outcomes.

Portfolio Drift and Market Dynamics

Portfolio drift is the natural change in asset weights caused by varying market performances over time. When certain spot assets outperform others, their market values increase, which automatically expands their percentage weights within your overall portfolio. Conversely, underperforming assets will shrink in weight. For instance, if you start with equal allocations in stocks and crypto, a major bull market in digital assets will quickly distort your balance, making your portfolio heavily weighted toward highly volatile cryptocurrency assets.

A price change alters marked weights even without an order. A hypothetical drift threshold can be a manual review condition; a breach is not automatically an instruction to trade. Consider the assumptions, exposures and costs. TradeHQ does not provide automatic allocation alerts; use a separate calculation and record any decision. No threshold fits every portfolio or ensures a particular outcome.

Worked Example: Drift in Action

Let us examine a detailed hypothetical scenario to see how portfolio drift operates in practice. Imagine you start with $100,000 in virtual cash and allocate fifty percent to a spot equity ETF and fifty percent to a major cryptocurrency. Your initial position values are fifty thousand dollars each. Over the course of a month, the equity ETF value remains unchanged at fifty thousand dollars, but the cryptocurrency surges by fifty percent, bringing its individual market value up to seventy-five thousand dollars.

At the hypothetical end date, $50,000 plus $75,000 gives $125,000. The weights are 40% and 60%. These are invented marked balances that exclude transaction costs and cash flows, not a return forecast. A higher token weight changes sensitivity to that token; the calculation alone does not require a trade or establish the safest allocation. A rebalancing comparison must add fees and alternative outcomes before drawing even a classroom conclusion.

Practice Task: Assessing Your Exposure

For this practice exercise, analyze a virtual portfolio that has drifted over several weeks of trading. Your initial setup consisted of $50,000 in spot gold, $30,000 in a global stock index, and $20,000 in a volatile token. Due to market movements, your gold is now worth $45,000, the stock index is worth $35,000, and the token has risen to $40,000. Calculate your new total portfolio value and determine the current percentage weight of each asset to identify drift.

The hypothetical end values total $120,000. Dividing each by that same denominator gives gold 37.5%, the index approximately 29.1667% and the token approximately 33.3333%. The token’s initial weight was 20%, so its weight rose by about 13.3333 percentage points. Percentage points differ from a percent change in the weight itself. These marked balances exclude costs and cash flows. The drift identifies changed exposure, not a universally unacceptable allocation or an automatic trade. Compare any chosen review threshold with the original assumptions and missing risks before evaluating a hypothetical rebalance.

KEY TAKEAWAYS
Concentration risk leaves a portfolio highly vulnerable to negative shocks in a single asset or sector.
Portfolio drift occurs naturally as market price movements change the relative weights of your assets over time.
Setting strict exposure limits and drift thresholds helps maintain an intentional risk profile.

Inactivity of the paper trading platform's databaseThe execution of limit orders at arbitrary pricesUnbalanced performance of different assets altering their weight percentagesDaily fees charged on spot trading simulator balances
3. If your target weight for a token is 15% and its current weight has drifted to 27%, what should you do to manage risk?

4. How is the total value of a spot portfolio calculated to determine asset weights?
